title: Memory Hierarchy and Locality
subtitle: Why sequential access wins and how 64 bytes shapes your code.
summary: Walk from registers to SSD, learn the 64-byte cache line, and measure why stride matters.
learning_objectives: Describe the hierarchy from registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → RAM → SSD with latency intuition.
Explain the 64-byte cache line and why sequential access is faster per byte.
Predict cache-line and TLB effects and name fixes like alignas(64) and huge pages.
prerequisites: Basic C and ability to compile hello.c

blocks.title: The key idea
blocks.markdown: The CPU never sees RAM directly. It sees registers (1 cycle), then caches that hide RAM's ~80 ns latency. A line is **64 bytes** — fetch one byte and you fetch 63 neighbours. Algorithms that respect this win by 10×.

Registers live on the core itself — tens of bytes, 1 cycle. L1 (32 KiB, ~4 cycles) and L2 (256 KiB, ~12 cycles) are per-core; L3 (8–32 MiB, ~40 cycles) is shared. Main memory is gigabytes at ~80 ns plus 4 KiB pages via the TLB. Storage (NVMe/SSD) is milliseconds-away by comparison. The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches virtual→physical page mappings; a TLB miss triggers a page walk (four memory reads on x64).

Programs that miss often do not wait for one miss — they wait for many. Good layout turns misses into hits.

blocks.explanation: Stride 1 touches every byte of each 64-byte line. Stride 16 (64 bytes) touches one int per line and wastes 60 bytes. Report time per element to see the per-line cost.
blocks.expected_output: seq 0.04s stride16 0.02s — but per element stride 16 is slower after normalising by elements touched

blocks.title: Numbers are approximate
blocks.markdown: L1 4c / RAM 80 ns / SSD 50 µs figures vary by chip and configuration. Use them as intuition, not datasheet. Measure on your machine with bench/cache-stride.c and note your own ratios.

blocks.title: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory (Ulrich Drepper)
blocks.purpose: Deeper reference for caches, VM, TLB and NUMA. Skim section 2–3 for this lesson.

blocks.question: Why is sequential array traversal usually faster per byte than strided traversal that skips 60 bytes each step?
options: The CPU has a special sequential instruction.
Each miss fetches a 64-byte line; sequential touches every byte of the line, strided wastes most of it.
Strided uses more power and throttles.
blocks.explanation: A cache miss loads a full 64-byte line. Sequential uses the whole line before the next miss; strided loads a line for 4 bytes and discards 60.

blocks.title: See the line size yourself
blocks.objective: Observe cache-line effects by varying stride and interpreting timing.
blocks.environment: C compiler with -O2; any desktop OS.
instructions: Compile and run cache-stride.c with -O2 and note both timings.
Divide each timing by number of elements visited to get per-element cost.
Change N to 1K and re-measure — does the advantage remain?
Look up your L1 size (32 KiB vs 48 KiB) and explain when the array stops fitting.
hints: Keep s volatile so the compiler does not optimise away the loop.
Try stride 8 (32 bytes) vs 16 (64 bytes) vs 32 (128 bytes) and plot.
completion_criteria: You report seq vs strided per-element cost
You explain why per-element cost rises at 64-byte stride
You note where L1/L2 would fit the working set
